pages.title: gateline — artifact-driven, human-gated agent pipelines
pages.description: gateline is an open-source framework for running the software development lifecycle as a team of semi-autonomous agents, with named humans approving at phase gates.

pages.title: How It Works
pages.description: The pipeline model end to end: the run lifecycle, the gates that keep a named human in charge, and the separation that keeps the framework vendor-neutral.

pages.title: How a run works
pages.blurb: One change, carried from a one-page brief to a merged branch: the four gates, the run directory as the whole of pipeline state, profiles, two-step creation, and the gate-less historian sweep.
pages.description: The G0–G3 run lifecycle, the run directory as pipeline state, profiles, two-step creation, and historian sweeps.

pages.title: How gates keep a human in charge
pages.nav: How gates keep a human in charge
pages.blurb: A prohibition built into the code rather than instructed: who may write a gate, how two writers share one file, what happens at a cap, and how autonomy is earned and measured.
pages.description: Structural gate authorship, the co-writer contract, round caps and escalation, one-authority topology, and the trust ladder.

pages.title: How gateline stays vendor-neutral
pages.blurb: Roles are contracts over files, models are bindings in a single registry, and adapters are rendered rather than written — with the cross-vendor decorrelation gradient stated honestly.
pages.description: Roles as contracts, the model registry, rendered adapters, and the honest per-adapter decorrelation gradient.

pages.title: Onboarding
pages.description: The fluency layer: the advanced topics gateline depends on but never explains, each taught through the place in the codebase where it does real work.

pages.title: Git, down to the plumbing
pages.blurb: Git as a small transactional database: the object store, compare-and-swap ref updates, reading files without a checkout, fast-forward-only as a policy primitive, and worktrees.
pages.description: Git's object model, CAS ref updates, checkout-free reads, fast-forward-only, and worktrees — taught where gateline relies on them.

pages.title: The co-written state file
pages.blurb: One file with two writers: normative comments, mutations as data, a single write path, refusal as a return value, and append-only facts with derived totals.
pages.description: How runs/<slug>/state.yaml is safely co-written by a human and the orchestrator.

pages.title: Contracts and their parsers
pages.blurb: Prose as a wire format: what a contract declares, the ID grammars and who parses them, why normative and parsed are independent, and how to evolve a contract safely.
pages.description: Artifact contracts as a two-audience format — the ID grammars, the READABILITY rule sets, and safe contract evolution.

pages.title: Reference
pages.description: Exact shapes for adopter tooling: the CLI surface, the state and orchestrator schemas, adapter manifests, and the artifact contract grammar.

pages.title: CLI reference
pages.blurb: Every gateline subcommand across the inspect, decide, create and serve groups, plus the gateline-orchestrator and gateline-runner-agent binaries.
pages.description: The gateline CLI surface: global flags, all subcommands, and the companion orchestrator and runner-agent binaries.

pages.title: state.yaml reference
pages.blurb: The run-state contract field by field: phases, profiles and their gate sets, gate entries, the budget ledger, tasks, escalations, and the co-writer rules.
pages.description: Field-by-field reference for runs/<slug>/state.yaml, the single source of truth for a pipeline run.

pages.title: orchestrator.yaml reference
pages.blurb: Schedules for periodic, gate-less role dispatches: the key shape, the interval grammar, where the engine reads the file, and the sweep derivation rules.
pages.description: The orchestrator.yaml schedule keys, interval grammar, and the S0–S4+SB sweep derivation rules.

pages.title: Adapter manifest reference
pages.blurb: The manifest schema key by key across the three shipped adapters, how gateline render consumes it, and the narrow-never-widen permission rule.
pages.description: The adapter manifest schema, the render pipeline that consumes it, and the permission model.

pages.title: Contract grammar reference
pages.blurb: The ten artifact contracts and their two normative rule families — ID/heading grammar and READABILITY — plus the human-vs-orchestrator commit-message grammar.
pages.description: The artifact contracts, their ID and READABILITY rule families, and the commit-message grammar.
